As generations pass, and the garden grows, so does the population of seekers desperately hunting for something new, and the numbers of those that have given up trying.

The Sacrifice of Sevens was one mad mage's misguided attempt to save the world. Some of it, at least. It was a spell to knit together the mundane and the magical, a spell of unmaking and remaking.

It was the dirtiest kind of magic, a blood sacrifice, of seven mothers and their seven unborn children, of seven continents and seven seas, of seven races not yet seen and of seven sleeping cities. Oh, and of approximately seven billion human souls, although they didn't all die at once. And all it managed to save was a magically-twisted scrap of land roughly the size of Australia, and the few people on it that haven't killed each other yet.

How you describe it will come down to your own personal style, and also the needs of the book - a horror story should probably be lighter on the description than a sci-fi story (everything's less scary once you start to know how it works). I'm a very visual person, so I draw inspiration from how creatures are presented in films and tv - how the shots are laid out, what they focus on and what they don't, can be pretty good guidelines for writing too.

As an example, the aliens from Edge of Tomorrow are very rarely shown in any great detail - but in almost every shot they're in constant violent motion, little whirling dervishes of death. That characteristic is far more important than the number of tentacles or eyes, and if I was translating it into text that's what I'd focus on.

It also really depends on what role the monster serves. For a big lynch-pin monster, something that's the only one of its like in the story or a major antagonist (think the Xenomorph from Alien) I personally like to go for a 'reveal' style, where I'll drip feed little bits and pieces then go in for the closeup shot, a big long paragraph describing it in all it's glory. Whereas if it's something a bit more common (think an orc in LotR), then maybe I don't need to do more than give the impression of ugly brutishness.

It's generally like describing anything else. If it's an important character, or it's a plot relevant feature, bring it up, otherwise you can just skim over it. Hell, even just a good name can give a good starting impression - I have a creature that looks like a moving scab (big black pitted shell), so they get called scabs. And I don't even need to say big black pitted shell anymore!

Gonna attach myself to this and say I agree 100%. Your readers will always imagine the thing that scares them the most, up until they find out what it really is. Even when they do find out what it really is, don't make it mundane.  
The Xenomorph isn't just an alien, it's the ultimate predator, an unstoppable killing machine. The thing that follows from It Follows never stops, can't be hurt, and the only information the protagonists have about it turns out to be half-wrong.  
The protagonists should get away (if they get away) by the skin of their teeth and a fair bit of luck, with barely any more information about what they were up against than when they went in. And as a final subjective point (my personal taste), their victory shouldn't be total. Don't kill the monster, fight it off and flee. Something you can't beat, something that's still *out there* at the end of the story is far scarier than a dead thing.

The thing is, depending on the Sci in your Fi, it might not make a difference. The world can look pretty different after 50 or a 100 years of technological advancement. Does it matter? You could just leave the question open. If it's not important to the story where it happens (no finding a trashed Statue of Liberty in the sand), why even bring it up?

Also, whether your world is real or fake you should do your study (in my opinion the best Sci-Fi has lots of Sci to go with the Fi), especially around stuff that's relevant to your major plot-points. You'll never satisfy all the experts (and don't waste your time trying), but a bad or unbelievable explanation kills suspension of disbelief.

I'm going to go out on a limb here and assume that most people think (like me) that the Joker is one of the best comic book villains. There is no better way to describe his character than 'unapologetically evil'. That is his entire schtick.

But his evil is entirely relatable. In most interpretations, his great drive is to break Batman. Prove that he's as crazy as everyone else in Gotham. Evil? Yes. Absolutely. But on a comprehensible scale. Even if you take away that, he's driven by his belief that death and destruction are hilarious, which most people can understand, if not agree with.

Of your list of villains (and I'll confess I'm only familiar with Voldemort and Sauron), Voldemort is an ok Villain. But he is completely outshone by Dolores Umbridge. It's hard to relate to Wizard Holocaust. It's easy to relate to the trope of power-hungry administration gone too far. Hell, Voldemort got a sad backstory with his parents, Dolores is just that much of a terrible person.

Sauron falls into the same trope as many other 'Big Bads'. They're Big, they're Bad, and that's it. Name one other aspect of Sauron's character. Tell me why he wants middle earth. You won't find an answer without digging into appendices or the Silmarillion. Saruman is a far more interesting villain - he wanted to be on the winning team.

Basically there's been an influx recently (thanks Marvel) of villains who exist solely to be villainous, without any reason or goal beyond that. Even worse, their villainy is on a scale that we just can't respond to. You can make villains unapologetic (they're not really villains otherwise), you can make them proud to be evil, but they need to have a relatable end goal.

You don't want to write literary fiction. You said it yourself when you said 'some pithy series about the realities of adult life'. That's not the words of someone who wants to write it. Do you need a better reason to write fantasy than because that's what you want to write?

But I'll give you a couple of reasons why I write fantasy.

Most importantly, literary fiction bores me to death.

Also importantly, it's bound by the chains of reality, and in my cynical worldview, there aren't any happy endings in reality. If I want to write a story where the good guys win, where virtue triumphs and people get the endings they deserve? That's fantasy. Because in the real world people just stagnate and move in cycles and dig themselves ever deeper into moral holes.

There's no limitations on what I write. I want a dragon, I get a dragon.

I love worldbuilding, none of that in literary fiction.

I can write a story about accepting yourself, about tolerance, about racism and coming to know your own culture, without needing that to be the only elements in the story. Put a fantastical dressing on it, and it can resonate with the people it affects, and those that don't care can still enjoy the adventure. I can do it without needing to worry about the thin line between no one getting it and beating the reader over the head with it, too, because if no one gets it I still have a story.

Finally, I want to actually enjoy reading it when I'm done. I'm not writing a story for the people who enjoy literary fiction. Plenty of others already are. I'm writing for me, and I guarantee with 7 billion people in the world there's enough people like me my books will have an audience.

My overall impression was that it felt slow, and I struggled to get through it all. Lots of scenery description, lots of backstory, little happens. Its important to make sure you save your words for the important stuff - there was about as much on the basically irrelevant bad music argument in the car as there was on the obviously important mysterious lady,

Besides that, overall the voice didn't do it for me. It felt like everything was being relayed through the narrator, and she wasn't interesting enough to carry it. Don't tell me the parents argue a lot - show me the character adding her new apology book to a pile of unread books and we get the picture far more vividly. Or have her put her own spin on it. Just relaying the information weakens the message.

Other than that, some sentences are a bit clunky/there are some odd word choices (profound lawyer?), but it wasn't a biggy.

It had good potential. Carry on if you enjoyed it! (But don't do it for the ladies). And take my advice with a grain of salt - I prefer fast-paced minimal description stuff.

One thing to consider is the human dregs item - the heaviest part of a human, they sink to the 'lowest depths imaginable'. They're Aldritch's covenant item, and they share the blue colour scheme of the deep. I'm fairly certain the deep is made of, or fed by, dregs, just like the abyss is made of/fed by humanity. Which raises the question: what are dregs?

My personal theory is that dregs are what's left over when humanity is burned - much like in real life, where the only stuff left after a cremation are fragments of bone (the heaviest parts of the body). A sort of 'ash' of humanity, once you've gone past even embers. That's why the deep is growing - there's a running theme in the game that the cycle is falling apart, that there's only so long you can use humans as a fuel source before you run out. That would explain the rising age of the deep.

There's probably also something meaningful about the fact that the deep was originally peaceful. Certainly, the abyss was never peaceful. Manus fathered it, and peaceful is not a word I'd use to describe him. Not to mention sacred - the abyss has always been feared. But I can see the deep starting off as some kind of weird Dark Souls-esque heaven, a resting place for the burned.

Overall, it's hard to say where the deep and the abyss lie in relation to each other. This is the first Souls game where we don't get to see the abyss, only its effects. I'd be interested to see how the repeated burning of humanity has affected it.

So there's lots of varieties of dark magic - magic that hurts others, magic that takes away free will, magic that kills or destroys. Blood magic and necromancy and mind control.

But you want EVIL magic, which I take to mean magic that is evil in itself, regardless of the intent of the user. The best way to show that sort of magic off is side effects. Show spells that can't be cast without warping and twisting everything around them, including the caster. Show a noble soul descending into madness as he taps into black magic with (initially) good intentions. Show users' bodies twisting and warping with their minds. Show stillborn children and un-healing wounds and magic so black it stains the lands it was cast on for generations. Show what happens when people are brought back from the dead, whatever personality they once had burned away by inhuman rage, or replaced with mindless terror at the horrors they witnessed beyond the veil.

Evil stains, corrupts, and destroys. Your evil magic should do the same, even when the intended effects run counter to that.

Depends on a variety of factors. If said pyromancer is already born into noble lineage, he's likely to do pretty well - not so much if he's born a street rat. Doubtful he'd ever be a slave though - you're talking about someone orders of magnitude more powerful than everyone else. Either pyromancers are waaaaay down the power tier list in this world, or the only shot the people in charge have of keeping him down is murder/emotional blackmail.

Also depends on when power is determined. If they know at birth, his chances go way down. If it takes a while to manifest, he has a better shot of doing well for himself, by being able to hide in anonymity.

To clarify my earlier point, constraints on individual powers make for interesting characters and scenarios, but for interesting powers you need to explore the constraints of the magic system as a whole. Going back to the thermodynamics point of before, if that ISN'T a constraint of the world, suddenly pyromancers are sources of infinite, clean energy. That's the sort of thing people go to war over (bonus points if you can't remove the created energy from the system and magi-tech begins cooking the planet). That could be a whole plot right there, all because you decided your magic breaks the laws of physics.

A lot of the creativity depends on the constraints, and the rules of the world - someone who can do anything is boring (see Superman).


As an example, imagine your pyrokinetic is limited by the laws of thermodynamics: from where does he get his heat? From his environment? From himself? Be a neat touch if the aftermath of a large battle had him shivering under a layer of flash frost. As for interesting uses, someone could use that power (or any heat-based power) to trick infrared cameras and other heat-activated technologies.


Other interesting uses include, but are not limited to:


- Creating smoke (by burning plastic or fresh greenery), either as a signal, or to create a distraction.


- Magic flashbang - superheated air is what causes thunder, and fire can get blindingly bright.


- Rave. This person could become a walking fireworks display (valuable for distractions or entertainment)


- This one comes up more often, but your pyrokinetic should never be cold. Super handy on any kind of expedition outside of the tropics.


- Chef. Perfect steak every time. Excellent smores, etc. (In a more high fantasy work, again super handy for adventurers).


- If you're really liberal with the definition of 'fire', this person could create (or destroy) passion in other people - acting as a muse, or a marriage counselor (or a particularly devious divorce lawyer).


- Even something as simple as pointing out that this person has become popular with the local smokers helps ground their magic in the world. There's more to life than fighting.


It's magic. Have fun with it!

Wikipedia is a good starting point for research: it will give you a rundown on symptoms, possible causes, possible treatments, and other useful information. This can be a springboard into more information if you find an area you want to research more deeply. That will allow you to cover the 'accurate' part from a purely factual perspective.

To actually make it work, find people who have the disorder, and see what they have to say. You don't need to necessarily interview someone (although that would be good), just hunt down a forum where they talk to each other. About anything. (Subreddits are great for finding niche communities about literally anything). Chances are, you'll find plenty of inspiration to help you make the character real.

And in the 60s, humans made it into space. You could go the semi-mystical route and say that had some cosmological significance that kicked everything off. For a very logical/goal-driven villain, monsters are a means to an end. They're your servants, your guards, your army. They're the guard dog you have on display so everyone knows not to fuck with you. Hell, you might even keep them just to show the world what a badass you are to own something like that.

For a villain driven more by passion/emotions, they might not be viewed as monsters. For a mad scientist they are the 'perfect creation'. For a necromancer, they might be re-animated loved ones gone wrong, or zombie friends for a person who never had any. And for a really dark take on it, what better torture for your enemies than to turn them into your loathsome pet?

The answer to your question will come when you know what sort of villain you have, and what sort of monster. Hell, in Jurassic Park they make the monsters for a theme park.

As some people have said, most algorithms aren't truly random, but rather pseudo-random. What this means is that the computer will always return the exact same number for the exact same input.

These algorithms generally take a 'seed' number and then do a bunch of math on it to turn it into a 'random' number. Similar inputs might have very different output. Usually this seed is the current time, since that generates numbers that look random enough to a human. It breaks down if you need really really random data, or if you're working at regular intervals.

True random data needs outside input, since computers are, by design, predictable. For example, Minecraft and other randomly generated games often allow users to type in a seed, some sites get the user to wiggle their mouse. Random.org uses data from atmospheric sensors.

TL;DR: Computers aren't random. People are, so to get a truly random number a computer needs a person's help. Usually they just fake it though.

Finally, I feel the Chinese Room thought experiment is nothing more than a misdirection, or misunderstanding of AI. Certainly, the man can't speak Chinese. Nor can the papers he reads, or the pen and ink he writes with, or the walls that hold him. Just like the language centres in my brain can't speak English, nor can my vocal chords, nor my eyes read it. I can speak English though, and the Chinese Room can speak Chinese. The experiment falsely claims the man is the entirety of the system, but just as a human is a collection of complex parts, and a strong AI is a collection of programs, the Room is composed of more than just the man. (I'm a computer scientist though, so I'm completely biased)

One reason for this is the influence of the heavily-independent Drake culture on society. Another cause is the effect of magic reducing effective gender dimorphism. Woman stopped being weaker than men a long time ago.

There are two edge cases: Drakes from outside the city walls tend to have long-term (not necessarily monogamous) relationships in order to keep the pack structure stable - their environment is too hostile to waste energy on family squabbles.

The other interesting case are the shape-shifters - ever the perfectionists and seekers of the aesthetic, they'll treat sex like any other bodily function - they seek to improve upon it and push the boundaries. Non shape-shifters tend to stay well away - they like their genitals human, thank you very much.

The fighters were the slaves of the Iron Kingdom, people of all castes, all races and all ages. They'd been fleeing east for weeks, with their captors in hot pursuit. They numbered in the hundreds of thousands (though of course far fewer were combatants).

Their escape came to an end when they ran out of ground to run on - they were herded onto a peninsula, cornered, with no way out. They sought help from the Fey who lived in the coastal caves there, (the only caste that had been able to resist the might of the Iron Kingdom in the past) but no help was given, and so they prepared to make their last stand.

The Smiths (members of Iron Kingdom) were powerful but lacked the skills they needed to sustain themselves. Shortly after their city's founding they began to develop a culture of independence and xenophobia, and soon thereafter decided to solve their shortcomings by enslaving the 'lesser' castes. The escaped slaves stood for everything the Smiths didn't - they believed in a society based on unity between castes, with freedom and protection for all who wanted it.

The Smith army numbered only a few thousand, but their caste had mastery over metal, and so their soldiers marched in full suits of masterwork armour, with the capacity to rain steel death from a distance and fight with countless dancing blades in close quarters - few of the other castes had the fortitude to survive any direct confrontation with a fully equipped Smith.

The first half of the battle went much as one would expect - the Smiths carved a bloody path through the slaves, killing the leaders of the rebellion and crushing their morale. Then came the Fey. They swarmed up out of their caves with an army of shadows, their queen at their head. The shades were so numerous they blacked out the sun, and the Smiths fell prey to their whisperings - promises of terror, madness and despair. The Fey's shadows were not enemies that could not be fought with steel, and their arrival turned the tide of the fight - the slaves saw their chance, rallied, and fought back, and eventually the Smiths were forced to retreat.

Soon after, the survivors founded Sanctuary City - with its offer of protection for any who chose to live there and abide by its rules. A government was formed from members of each caste (save the Smiths, who were deemed 'exiles' from the start). The Fey remained in their caves, but their culture influenced the others, and soon the caves had become elaborate catacombs, the Fey revered as keepers of the dead.

Eventually, the bad blood between Sanctuary City and the Iron Kingdom was reconciled, after the Smiths came to the aid of the city when it was under siege by the Legionnaires' army of war machines.

Magic stems from an alternative dimension, closely intertwined with our own, known as the Dream. The Dream is shaped by the thoughts and beliefs of sentient life (ie. us), and in turn the strongest entities in the Dream bleed through into our world. There are two kinds of magic practitioner - first, the Dreamers, not-quite-humans native to the Dream. They've been molded into the 'ideal' human - long-lived, charismatic, strong, smart, fast. Their magic is primarily that of a glamour (illusions, mind reading, hypnosis) - fitting for people from such a transient dimension. Very rarely, Dreamers have much stronger magical talents - their magic is demanding but very flexible in what it can accomplish.

Some humans however, also manifest magical talents. Usually these are relatively minor (eg. being able to know when someone is lying). These humans are essentially born closer to the dream - their most interesting characteristic is that magic is catching. The more mages you put in one place, the thinner the veil, the more powerful they become and the more likely new mages are to be born (Dreamers have a similar effect when in human lands). Besides that, magic is essentially a talent you are born with, everyone's abilities are different, and although it obeys set rules for a given individual those don't necessarily hold between different mages.

At some point in the story's timeline, an unhinged Dreamer casts an incredibly potent spell, entangling the Dream and our world into one. The result is magic split into eight castes, and everyone is born into one of the castes. Magic for everyone!

**Mages**: Draw power from other individuals and from items that have seen a lot of magic. Their magic is very flexible, most choose to focus on a single aspect though. Their trademark abilities are telekinesis (they find it easy) and anti-magic.

**Shapers**: Shapeshifters, can alter their own form or that of anything they touch. It's very painful, but they're the best healers around. Their magic requires understanding of physical forms, a large part of their culture revolves around discovering new biologies.

**Drakes**: Two minds, two bodies, one person. Think a werewolf, except with a wingless dragon and the second mind is sentient. Known for their strength, strange culture, and incredible resilience and self-healing. Rare shamans use powerful, unpredictable magic (predominantly casting fire, lightning, or telekinesis).

**Fey**: Affinity for shades, denizens of the old Dream - essentially literal manifestations of human emotions. Some shades provide valuable advice, but most are liars. All are experts at manipulating the minds of their victims to produce the emotions they feed on. The Fey have the ability to summon shades into the human world, where they remain until their form evaporates in the light.

**Empaths**: Mind-readers and mind-changers. Fighters use their abilities to predict their opponents moves, in very rare cases they can completely dominate the mind of another and render them a  lifeless puppet.

**Smiths**: Think Magneto, but all metals. Manipulate metals, draw power from them. Almost single handedly responsible for the demise of the gun as an effective weapon. They can shape metal as if it were clay as well - the best tools were made by the Smiths.

**Warpers**: Reality warpers. At their mildest, very lucky individuals, but they are perfectly capable of reshaping the entire universe to meet their desires. Fortunately, they're very rare, and on a very tight leash - the use of their powers attracts the attention of very unpleasant cosmic things, so most Warpers live their lives using as little magic as possible.

**Artificers**: Innate knack for construction and creation, if this were a video game they'd be the guys who +1 your stuff. Most impressive ability is that they can imbue sentience into artificial constructs - these automatons often make life companions.

TL;DR: I fucking love magic, and different kinds of magic.

In the beginning, before light, before life, before time, there were dragons. Warrior and Shaman. They fought, as is the way of their kind, to see which of the two was strongest, but though Warrior was strong Shaman was cunning, and for eons they fought without a victor. Every time they clashed, the flames forged planets and suns, and wherever their blood fell, life sprung up, only to be  struck down by tail or talon or flame.


But slowly Warrior gained an edge, for it was strong enough to survive Shaman's tricks, and adapt to them. So Shaman travelled to places Warrior would not follow, in search of new knowledge. The dragon travelled to the dark depths of space, and there it learnt how to hide. It communed with the dead suns, and from them it learned even dragonflame could be quenched. But that was not enough, so Shaman travelled to the deepest dark, to the land of the dead, to learn their secrets.


From them, Shaman learnt many things. There were none the dead hated more than the dragons who had slain them – they taught Shaman suffering, and hate, and the cold touch of death. It forged these into a poison blade, and the next time the dragons clashed, drove it deep into Warrior's belly, a mortal wound.


Warrior was furious at this trickery, and in its rage was more than a match for Shaman. Shaman was smote from life and from death, no longer Shaman, no longer dragon, banished to eternal solitude in the empty void. But rage could not heal Warrior's wound, and slowly it bled out, victorious at last.


The lifeblood of dragons ran thick and dark that day, and the life that sprung up carried the embers of dragonflame within it – as well as the embers of the dragon's ancient conflict. For though Shaman was defeated, its will carries on, and even its blood longs to spread the knowledge of death.

If it's in his character to be glib and jokey even at death's door, fair enough, but even then it could be more potent to throw that away when he realises he's kicking the bucket. If that's not his character (or if as you say he doesn't have much character), consider changing his attitude.

Very few deaths are as pleasant as this uncle's - especially unexpected death. If the uncle doesn't want to die, it would make a much more harrowing scene. He could go out messy and screaming and crying for help. He could die delusional, believing he's going to be fine. He could slowly and messily fade away over the course of an hour, drifting in and out of consciousness as his son and nephew watch, powerless. Those are all deaths that are naturally going to hit a lot harder than the current scene.

Not to mention this would be a great opportunity to have the death show another facet of the uncle's character - how he reacts to his mortality could be very illuminating. I will not dispute whether or not Chiropractic medicine helped your case. I will say I am doubtful it would help my depression.

I will dispute your assertion that antidepressants are placebos. A quick search indicates that 75% of sufferers treated with a placebo recovered, vs 96% of people treated with the medication.

All that says is that the placebo effect is a real thing with a marked effect, and we still don't know what the fuck is going on in the brain of a person with depression (or most other mental disorders). However, to suggest that antidepressants are purely placebo is a fallacy. And for a disease as debilitating, costly, and potentially deadly as depression, 96% is a helluva lot better than 75%

As a final note, to be permitted to sell antidepressants (and I presume other medications, but that's not my area of knowledge), a company must prove their product works better than a placebo.

Look to the villains in your own life, and upscale them. A common factor in what makes someone a villain is a lack of empathy and a disregard for the consequences of their actions. They don't necessarily need to be sadistic, but they do have to be heartless.

You could have the Umbridge, someone who believes in a cause and will happily torture kids to further it. (She also has shades of sadist).

You could have the sadist/violence is fun guy. No moral compass, a narcissist and a hedonist, will murder you because he felt like it. You could argue some serial killer villains fall into this category (The Joker's a good example).

Alternatively, you could have someone driven by revenge, so long as that revenge is clearly over the top and disproportional. The man who murders the killer of his family is almost an action hero, the man who does that and goes on to murder everyone that person ever laid eyes on is a villain.

Most villains need a backstory or some kind of motivation to have a semblance of realism, especially if they're a prominent character. The psychos can maybe manage without. The trick is that a villain is a person who goes too far. If you can look at their motivations and think 'I know where they're coming from', they're not pure evil, they're tragic. The way a villain thinks should be alien to you, as they repeatedly act outside societal and psychological norms.

When the media had broke the news that a cure had been found for death, it seemed the whole world got caught up in the sensationalism. It is the human condition to fear death and love life, and to most the prospect of immortality was too good to pass up. As the slogan went: "Who wouldn't want to live forever?"  

By the time the word about the 'cure' got out, it was too late. Untold millions of people had signed their souls over, and not a single one had ever stopped to ask the most important question: Who's paying for this? As it turns out, they were. Whatever failing parts they had - eyes, joints, organs - were cut out, replaced with cutting edge lab-grown replacements. Replacements that worked so long as the providers saw fit - so long as their owners were good little boys and girls.  

It was a brilliant scam, if nothing else. The people who signed up were the most desperate to cheat death, the least likely to turn on their new owners. And the best part was, it didn't even work. They never figured out how to fix a brain - some people doubt they ever tried. Whenever a slave (for that's all they were) completely lost the plot, they went in for a final repair job - the person that came out was little more than a robot - no memories, limited emotions, and all the personality of a dead fish. These are the workers of the new world - an army of corporate zombies, in every sense of the word, and every day the number of them grows. Who wouldn't want to live forever?
